title: OpenAI 称其 AI 解决了 Kakeya 猜想，数学家仍需解释其中缘由
author: Abdullahi Dattijo

AI Math Proofs Aren't Knowledge Until Someone Explains Them

From the Four Color Theorem to OpenAI's October 2026 claims, why computer-checked proofs still need people to explain, test, and extend them.

Abdullahi Dattijo
November 23, 202611 min read
Prefer us on Google

A discovery nobody has fully explained

On 22 July 1976, two mathematicians named Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken said they had proved the Four Color Theorem. The theorem is about coloring a map with only four colors so that no two places next to each other have the same color. Mathematicians had tried to prove that for more than a hundred years.

You cannot check every possible map one by one, so Appel and Haken broke the problem down into a long list of small maps to check. Their computer ran for more than a thousand hours to check all of those small maps, as Robin Wilson’s account in the Notices of the American Mathematical Society describes.

Many mathematicians at the time were unhappy with that kind of proof. Before 1976, a proof meant something another mathematician could read on paper and check by hand from start to finish, and here nobody could check the computer’s part by hand.

Other teams later wrote their own computer programs to check the same cases, and their programs agreed that four colors work. Still, many mathematicians wanted to know why four colors work without a huge computer check, and OpenAI’s October 2026 math announcements reminded me of that old argument.

On 26 October 2026, OpenAI announced three results that it says its AI models came up with. In the first one, OpenAI says its model disproved the Exponential Time Hypothesis, an old belief about how fast a computer can solve a hard kind of logic puzzle. In the second one, OpenAI says its model settled the Kakeya conjecture, an open problem about shapes and waves.

In the third one, OpenAI says its model proved that the math behind quantum chromodynamics, which describes the strong force holding an atom’s nucleus together, has no contradictions in it. Physicists have used that theory for decades without a proof that its equations hold together, and OpenAI says its proof covers a larger part of particle physics too.

OpenAI calls all three of these results discoveries in its post. At the same time, OpenAI says the model papers are only a starting point, and that human scientists still have to read them and figure out what they mean.

OpenAI also asked outside researchers to read the model papers and help explain them. Even if the proofs turn out to be right, other mathematicians still must check them and see what they mean, since right now they are company claims.

When an AI model gives an answer that nobody can explain yet, has science actually moved forward?

Knowing is not understanding

When a mathematician reads a proof on paper, the proof does more than say a claim is true. Reading the steps also shows why the claim is true, and often gives the reader a trick to try on a different problem.

OpenAI says its disproof of the Exponential Time Hypothesis was checked in a computer tool called Lean within a day. Lean checks whether every step follows the rules of logic, though a person still must check that the question typed into Lean matches what mathematicians meant to ask.

Even when a computer checks every line, people can still walk away without understanding the main idea. Thomas Hales ran into that in 1998 with the Kepler conjecture on stacking round balls. The journal’s reviewers said they were 99 percent sure Hales was right, yet they could not check every part by hand.

Hales and his team then worked until 2014 to put the whole Kepler proof into a computer-checked form from start to finish. Reading about Hales’s long effort made me think that checking whether a proof is right and explaining why it works are two different jobs.

Knowing that a statement is true is not always enough to help the next researcher. People in the field still have to figure out how the new proof fits with what they already know, and whether the same idea works on other questions.

When answers become cheap

On 9 October 2026, the mathematician Terence Tao gave a talk at Caltech, and the next day he put up a short blog post called Math 2.0. As I read his post, Tao thinks people focus too much on AI solving famous problems alone, rather than helping mathematicians understand and use math together.

I would go a little further than Tao does in that post. If AI models turn out proofs faster than people can read them, the hardest job for human researchers may be explaining those proofs and picking what to ask next.

Proving a famous old problem gets the news stories, while explaining someone else’s hard proof usually does not. If AI models put out more proofs that are hard to follow, the researchers who sit down and explain them will deserve much more credit than they get today.

Who gets the credit?

Suppose an AI model writes a proof, one group checks the steps, a second group explains the main idea, and a third group uses it on a new problem. Which group made the discovery, and who takes the blame if someone later finds a mistake in the paper?

Naming only whoever produced the first result leaves most of that work out.

Some people have already tried to answer. OpenAI says it will not claim academic credit for what its models produced. Instead, it says the teams of independent researchers it asked to study the results should get recognition for the explanations and writeups they produce.

The Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics takes a firmer line. It was published on 2 June 2026 and is endorsed by the International Mathematical Union.

It says human authors stay fully responsible for their results, and that credit belongs to people and not automated systems. It also says results belong in journals reviewed by other scientists, and that press releases and blog posts cannot replace the checking done by other scientists.

Together, those statements leave me wondering how credit and responsibility will be assigned in practice. If a paper is wrong, someone needs to correct the record; if researchers make it useful, their work needs recognition too. A 2026 dispute shows how hard that can be.

The mathematicians Tristan Buckmaster of New York University and Levent Alpöge, who works at Anthropic, another AI company, posted three proofs about equations that describe how fluids move. NYU describes one of them, a result about the Euler equations, which describe a simplified fluid with no friction. In that result, a fluid pushed by a gradually changing force can build up a spin that becomes infinitely fast after a limited time.

Reports say they used AI tools, mainly OpenAI’s coding tool Codex. Their Euler result is related to the Navier-Stokes problem, a famous question about how fluids move with a $1 million prize, but it does not solve it. Buckmaster says their approach, pushing the fluid with a gradually changing force, was unusual, and that as far as he knows hardly anyone else was working on it.

Soon after they posted their proofs, OpenAI announced its own result on the Navier-Stokes problem, also using a force that changes gradually. TechCrunch reported Buckmaster’s claim that OpenAI learned of their progress before it was public. OpenAI denies this, saying neither its researchers nor its AI systems saw the pair’s work, and that it does not intend to claim the prize.

Buckmaster also raised the concern that his heavy use of OpenAI’s Codex tool could have helped OpenAI’s models get better. OpenAI first called that unlikely but possible, then said after an investigation that his prompts could not have had any effect on its system. I cannot judge who is right.

The dispute raises a question for me. If a researcher’s work might help improve a company’s model, how should that contribution be recognized?

Who decides what is worth asking?

A study called HybridQuestion asked AI agents and human researchers to vote for the top breakthroughs of 2025, which had already happened, and the top open questions for 2026. The AI agents were all one AI model, told to act like different kinds of researchers, such as graduate students and professors. The humans were 30 graduate students and, in a second round, 10 professors.

When professors voted, the AI agents picked more of the same favorites as the humans for breakthroughs than for questions. For example, a question about building shared standards for evaluating AI got 7 votes from the professors and none from the AI agents. The study reported this comparison only for artificial intelligence.

The difference between those two tasks matters because a researcher choosing a question has to decide where to spend time and resources before knowing what the answer will be. Agreement about past breakthroughs does not necessarily tell us how well an AI system can make that choice. The study itself suggests that human experts probably disagree more with each other about future questions too.

As AI systems become more capable, researchers will still need to decide which questions deserve attention. I would want those choices to involve people who will live with the consequences.

More results are not more progress

AlphaFold, an AI system from Google DeepMind, predicts the shapes of proteins so well that two of its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The AlphaFold database contains more than 200 million predicted protein structures.

Those predictions are valuable to researchers. A predicted shape, though, does not by itself explain why a protein folds that way.

Mathematics now has a different problem, the number of results. Nature reported that OpenAI posted more than 700 unreviewed mathematical papers on 6 October 2026, and about three weeks later OpenAI announced three further results. Who reads all of it?

Science depends on people reviewing, testing and arguing about results. That work takes time, and a larger collection of results can create more for researchers to examine.

I worry that results could arrive faster than researchers can verify and understand them. A long list of papers would then look like progress even if few of them are understood.

The case against my view

The strongest answer to everything above is that science has never required every researcher to understand every result. Medicine already works this way. Doctors recommend acetaminophen, a common pain reliever, even though a 2021 paper says how it works is still not fully understood after decades of research.

Engineering is similar. A 2016 IEEE Spectrum review of the book Overcomplicated says the complexity of modern technology has passed a point where no single person can fully understand a complete system. Teams still build and use these systems, even though no member knows every detail.

A proof that a computer has verified step by step is valuable even if few people can explain it. An AI system may also find connections that no human would have found in a lifetime. I accept that, and I would not want to throw those results away.

Researchers can use a result before they fully understand it. My concern is that, without an explanation, they may not know where the result applies, where it fails, or how to build on it.

Five questions to ask of every AI result

Checking that an AI proof has no mistakes in its steps is only the first check. When I read about a new AI result in science, there are five questions I want answered.

  1. Is the result actually right?

  2. Can other scientists check the work on their own without private company tools?

  3. Does the paper help people see why the answer is true?

  4. Can another researcher take the idea and use it on a different problem?

  5. Does the result open up a new question worth spending time on?

Each of those five questions looks for a different gap. A proof can be right in every step while nobody knows why it works, or easy to follow while giving other researchers nothing they can use in their own work.

Not every good paper has to do all five things at once. Still, asking all five helps tell the difference between a result that a computer has checked and a result that people have understood and put to work.

People who work in data science see a similar problem when a model finds a strong pattern in a table of numbers. Finding the pattern in the numbers does not tell you what caused it, so a person still has to look into why the pattern is there.

Who makes it knowledge?

Fifty years after Appel and Haken proved the Four Color Theorem in 1976, some mathematicians are still looking for a simpler reason why four colors are always enough. I think researchers will see the same thing happen with proofs that come out of AI models, even when a tool like Lean says every step is right.

My own answer to the question in the title is that human researchers are the ones who turn a bare result into knowledge. People still have to check the work, explain the main idea, argue about where it falls short, and connect it to other work, which takes time.

If AI models give science more results to read through, I hope the researchers who do the slow work of explaining them get the time and credit they deserve.
